title: Basic Lupine Urology

jokes.text: Opening Law & Order narration parody: 'Greendale Community College is represented by two separate, yet equally important types of people: The goofballs that run around stirring up trouble, and the eggheads that make a big deal out of it. These are their stories.'
jokes.setup: The iconic Law & Order opening narration format ('represented by two separate, yet equally important groups... these are their stories') is one of the most recognizable cold opens in TV history.
jokes.punchline: Applied to Greendale: 'goofballs that stir up trouble' and 'eggheads that make a big deal out of it' — deflating the gravitas of the original with community-college pettiness.
jokes.explanation: The joke earns its high score because it's not just a parody — it's a thesis statement for the entire episode's conceit. The word choices ('goofballs' vs. 'eggheads') perfectly mirror the Law & Order cadence while deflating it with mundane community-college specificity. Exceptional economy and structure — the whole genre parody is established in two sentences. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing you appreciate how precisely the rhythm is replicated before being subverted.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: In the criminal justice system, community-based offenses are considered especially heinous. At Greendale Community College, the students who commit these offenses are sent to a special imaginary unit known as the Campus Police. These are their stories.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Greendale Community College: where the goofballs and eggheads collide in a deadly mix of ignorance and haughty resentment.

jokes.text: Jeff's dentist non sequitur: 'She was perfect. Warm, smart, beautiful. I'm never gonna find another dental hygienist like that.' / 'Well, you should stop hitting on her.' / 'Hey, she's the one putting her hands in my mouth.'
jokes.setup: Jeff laments losing someone described in romantic, idealized terms ('warm, smart, beautiful') — sounds like a breakup.
jokes.punchline: It's a dental hygienist he was hitting on; and his defense is that she's 'the one putting her hands in my mouth' — classic Jeff rationalizing sleaziness with sophistry.
jokes.explanation: Strong misdirection — the romantic framing snaps into a mundane professional relationship. The punchline is very Jeff: he doesn't deny hitting on her, he reframes it as a contextual inevitability. Character integration is high because only Jeff would justify this specific behavior this way. Slightly undercut by being a cold-open throwaway not tied to the episode's main plot.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not proud of it, but every time I go to the dentist, I flirt with the hygienist. It's just my thing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: She leans in close, her hands are in my mouth, she tells me I need to floss more... it's basically foreplay.

jokes.text: 'Our yam was murdered.'
jokes.setup: Jeff just said he expected more than a yam after being summoned about a 'murder.'
jokes.punchline: Annie doubles down with complete sincerity: 'Our yam was murdered.' Zero irony. Full commitment.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum comedic density. The joke is entirely in Annie's earnest delivery of an objectively absurd statement. Character integration is high — Annie's hypercompetitive academic sincerity is her defining trait, and applying it to a yam is the perfect Annie move. Economy score of 9.5 because it cannot be shorter.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Nothing to see here.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: For once, there literally is nothing interesting.

jokes.text: Shirley takes command: 'You let me handle the nitty gritty. In the meantime, I need somebody to drum up suspects. You boys, canvas for witnesses...' — the study group snapping into cop-show mode instantly.
jokes.setup: The yam is 'killed' and the group needs to investigate. Shirley steps up.
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately slides into full Law & Order procedural mode — 'canvas for witnesses, establish a time frame and motive' — with zero irony, as if this is a completely normal response to a yam.
jokes.explanation: Functional genre-parody comedy — the joke is the gap between procedural seriousness and yam stakes. Shirley's character is well-served because her maternal authority translates amusingly into cop-show boss energy. Loses points for economy because the bit runs a touch long without a sharp punchline landing.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: A C? A C?! That's like... that's like getting pregnant as a teenager!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Nobody plans for it, everybody judges you, and you're stuck with it for the rest of your life!

jokes.text: 'It's been a long 15 years.' / 'Looks like it's gonna be a late night.' / 'How'd we manage to pull the short straw?' / 'It's not a short straw. It's a hot potato.' / 'Yeah, well, looks pretty cold to me.'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are assigned the investigative legwork and start doing cop-show banter.
jokes.punchline: They trade clichéd cop-show non sequiturs ('It's been a long 15 years'), mix their idioms ('short straw/hot potato'), and riff off each other with performative awareness.
jokes.explanation: Troy and Abed's buddy-cop banter is a highlight of the episode's premise — they're not just doing the genre, they're reveling in it. 'It's been a long 15 years' as a weary-cop line from a 20-year-old is a great absurdist beat. The 'hot potato/cold' wordplay chain is clever without being showy. Rewatch bonus because it's so joyful. Character integration is high because only Troy and Abed could make this feel like earnest play rather than cynical parody.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: This whole murder investigation is a distraction from what really matters - my stories.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: Now if you'll excuse me, I have a very important episode of 'Cops and Donuts' to watch.

jokes.text: Cut to Troy holding the destroyed yam and saying 'Cold? Or dead?' — reaction beat to his own 'looks pretty cold to me' line.
jokes.setup: Troy just said the hot potato 'looks pretty cold to me' as a cop-show line.
jokes.punchline: He looks at the yam and delivers 'Cold? Or dead?' — a one-man CSI moment that also lampshades the fact that cold and dead aren't mutually exclusive for a yam.
jokes.explanation: Perfect mini-callback — Troy follows his own setup with a beat that works both as genre parody (the CSI detective musing over a victim) and as genuine wordplay (a yam being literally cold and metaphorically dead). Economy is excellent. The four-second pause implied before this delivery makes the structure tighter.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Alright people, listen up. We've got a case to crack and I'm taking point on this investigation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We're going to need to shake down some witnesses, play good cop bad cop, and get down to brass tacks.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This perp isn't going to know what hit 'em. We're going full detective mode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, we're looking for who ate the last donut in the study room.

jokes.text: 'Survey says...' / 'We can't both do the zinger.' / 'Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Both Troy and Abed try to deliver the same CSI-style one-liner simultaneously.
jokes.punchline: They acknowledge the collision: 'We can't both do the zinger' — meta-commentary on the genre conventions they're performing.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest meta joke up to this point. The humor has two layers: (1) the collision itself is funny because they're so synchronized they can't even improv without matching, and (2) the clinical term 'zinger' makes explicit that they know they're in a genre and are navigating its conventions. 'Sorry' as the button is perfect — it's so mundane after the meta-commentary. High character integration because Troy and Abed's synchronized behavior is core to their friendship.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We got a yam case. It's cold. Real cold.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The dame at the farmer's market said it came in Tuesday. But nobody's seen it since.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: In this business, yams don't just disappear. They get disappeared.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're gonna need to go deeper. Much deeper.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I've worked homicide. I've worked vice. But I've never seen anything like this yam case.

jokes.text: 'Okay, okay, five-to-one on the black guy.' / 'That's offensive.' / 'Fine, six-to-one.'
jokes.setup: The group is about to question suspects. Pierce is apparently running odds on who's guilty.
jokes.punchline: Pierce's racism is immediately called out by Troy ('That's offensive') but Pierce's response isn't to retract — it's to adjust the odds, as if the offensiveness is a negotiating factor.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce joke structure: offensive premise + escalation that reveals the character hasn't processed the critique at all. The punchline 'Fine, six-to-one' is excellent because it shows Pierce heard 'offensive' as a bargaining position, not a moral objection. The structure is tight — three lines, maximum revelation of character. High character integration because this is precisely how Pierce's oblivious racism manifests in the show.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: This assignment is a hot potato we need to handle with kid gloves.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So we're juggling potatoes while wearing mittens?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, it's just a metaphor—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because I can't feel anything through these gloves. The potato is already cold.

jokes.text: Pierce interrogation: 'Did you hold it or drop it?' — after Pierce says he 'holds up his end'
jokes.setup: Pierce insists 'I hold up my end' regarding the yam-watering duty
jokes.punchline: Troy/Abed pounce: 'Did you hold it or drop it?' — turning Pierce's idiom against the literal crime
jokes.explanation: Decent wordplay — catches the double meaning quickly. A bit too easy to land as a great joke but functions well in the rapid-fire interrogation rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're giving me the cold shoulder.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not giving you anything.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're freezing me out.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You've murdered me. You've murdered me dead.

jokes.text: Pierce claiming he watered the yam, then being caught in a lie: 'I lied about watering it. I got there too late, the doors were already locked.' / 'Why were you late?' / 'I... fell asleep in a sunbeam.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is questioned about watering the yam — he claims he did it, then admits he didn't under pressure.
jokes.punchline: 'I fell asleep in a sunbeam' — the most Pierce explanation possible, delivered with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The 'fell asleep in a sunbeam' line is both specific enough to be hilarious and completely believable for Pierce — it conjures an image of a large, aging man splayed out on a carpet in afternoon sun. Character integration is a 9 because this is pitch-perfect Pierce. Britta's follow-up ('I used to live with him, it's kind of adorable') elevates it further, turning it from a one-liner into a character-revealing moment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're done here.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're done here.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You can't just say the same thing I said.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Why not? Cop shows do it all the time. Two characters say the exact same line for dramatic effect.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's... actually a fair point.

jokes.text: Britta's confirmation: 'Actually it is. I used to live with him, it's kind of adorable.'
jokes.setup: Troy says 'Likely story' about Pierce falling asleep in a sunbeam.
jokes.punchline: Britta neutrally confirms it's not unlikely at all — she's lived with Pierce and it's apparently a known, cute behavior. The word 'adorable' applied to Pierce is unexpected.
jokes.explanation: A good supporting laugh — the callback to Pierce and Britta's past living arrangement is a nice continuity gag, and 'kind of adorable' reframes Pierce's obliviousness as endearing rather than infuriating. Functions well as a tag to the sunbeam joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'll give you 3-to-1 odds the culprit is whoever looks the most suspicious.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And by suspicious, I mean different from me.

jokes.text: Todd's interrogation: 'In Iraq, keeping a tight schedule saved lives.' / 'Ah, what happened, Todd? Cut yourself on an extra sharp Oscar Wilde play?'
jokes.setup: Todd invokes his military service to explain his precise schedule during the interrogation.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's dismissive sarcasm — 'Cut yourself on an extra sharp Oscar Wilde play?' — is a preemptive dig at Todd's bandaged hand, delivered with Jeff's particular brand of contemptuous wit.
jokes.explanation: The Oscar Wilde reference is unexpected and specific — it implies Todd is a soft intellectual playing soldier, while also being a genuinely weird image. 'Extra sharp Oscar Wilde play' is a memorable phrase construction. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing you know the injury IS from a yam, making Jeff's preemptive mockery accidentally almost accurate.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I didn't mean it like that. I'd say the odds of me being racist are like one in a thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. One in five hundred.

jokes.text: Todd's muffin exchange: 'What kind of muffin?' / 'Blueberry.' / 'Why not raisin?' / 'That wasn't the assignment.'
jokes.setup: Todd explains his bandage is from a muffin burn in home ec. The interrogators press him on muffin specifics.
jokes.punchline: The interrogation goes granular on muffin variety, Todd answers straight ('That wasn't the assignment'), and the whole exchange performs the Law & Order habit of treating trivial details like crucial evidence.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best absurdist beats. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the procedural absurdity of interrogating someone about muffin variety, (2) Todd's straight 'That wasn't the assignment' — which is simultaneously the most and least informative answer possible, and (3) the implicit question of why raisin would even be more suspicious. The structure is perfect: escalating absurdity, then Todd's perfectly mundane deflation. High originality because the specific comedic mechanism (muffin variety as interrogation point) is genuinely novel.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I am Pierce Hawthorne, and I have come to destroy you all!

jokes.text: 'You can dance all day, Todd, but sooner or later, the music's gonna change.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is interrogating Todd in mock-cop fashion and delivers a warning.
jokes.punchline: The line is a perfect genre-convention cliché — the kind of vague threatening metaphor TV detectives deliver — applied to a yam investigation. Jeff delivers it with total conviction.
jokes.explanation: A solid procedural-cliché joke that works because Jeff commits fully. The line itself is the kind of meaningless tough-guy metaphor that sounds menacing but on inspection means nothing — which is exactly the joke. Character integration works because Jeff loves meaningless rhetoric.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I was late because I was napping in a sunbeam on my windowsill.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? Don't you people nap in sunbeams?

jokes.text: Todd's photo with clock: Abed transfers the photo and applies an 'old west color' filter.
jokes.setup: The group wants to verify Todd's alibi photo to establish the time the biology room was locked.
jokes.punchline: Abed processes the image and applies 'old west color' — a sepia filter — as if this is a legitimate forensic technique. It's a parody of CSI's absurd image-enhancement scenes.
jokes.explanation: CSI's 'enhance' gag is well-worn, but this iteration is fresh: the parody isn't of enhancement but of *arbitrary filtering* as analysis. 'Old west color' is a perfect specific absurdity — it has zero forensic value and Abed knows it, but he presents it with the same gravity a TV tech would use. The visual gag (the sepia-toned yam photo) is implied but clear. Rewatch bonus because the moment is lovingly dumb.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, no, it's real. Pierce told us about it. It happened.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: He's adorable.

jokes.text: 'I don't know. I thought it was cool.' (Abed's reaction to his own 'old west color' filter)
jokes.setup: Abed applies an unnecessary old-west sepia filter to the evidence photo.
jokes.punchline: The implied confused reaction from the group leads to Abed simply saying 'I don't know. I thought it was cool.' — dropping the procedural pretense entirely.
jokes.explanation: The button on the filter gag. What makes this exceptional is that Abed completely abandons the genre frame — in a show where he's usually the most committed genre participant — to admit he just thought it looked neat. The sincerity ('I thought it was cool') is funnier than any in-character justification would have been. High economy (seven words) and high character integration because Abed's combination of genre mastery and aesthetic nerdiness is perfectly expressed here.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, obviously, it's the study group's enemies. Or as I like to call them, the 'haters-and-doubters-inium.' It's a word I just made up. Sounds profound, doesn't it?

jokes.text: 'Eight plus two times five...' / 'Ten after 8:00.' / 'I'm gifted in other ways.'
jokes.setup: Britta tries to calculate what a clock reading means from the photo. Annie solves it instantly.
jokes.punchline: Britta's pre-emptive defense — 'I'm gifted in other ways' — before anyone even mocks her, delivered with practiced resignation.
jokes.explanation: Solid Britta self-deprecation joke. The humor is in her getting there before anyone else can pile on — she's internalized the group dynamic enough to pre-empt the mockery. Character integration is high because Britta's combination of incompetence and self-aware dignity is her defining comedic trait.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What happened to your face?

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: Oh, I cut myself shaving.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's a pretty bad cut. Were you using a razor or Oscar Wilde's sharp wit?

jokes.text: Annie starts to explain how she can help as a psych major and is immediately cut off mid-sentence.
jokes.setup: Annie volunteers: 'As a psych major, I could pr...'
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts or she's interrupted mid-word — the joke is that no one cares about psych major insights, a running gag about the uselessness of psychology as a discipline.
jokes.explanation: Functional running-gag territory — the dismissal of psych major utility is a Community staple. This instance is lighter because it doesn't have a sharp punchline, just a cut. The humor relies on the audience recognizing the pattern.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What kind of muffin was it?

jokes.text: Dramatic pause reveal: 'Monday night, one biology room key checked out by... [pause] ...Magnitude.'
jokes.setup: Classic detective-show dramatic revelation pause — the music cues, the name is about to drop
jokes.punchline: The name is 'Magnitude' — a minor background character known for saying 'Pop pop!' — maximally anticlimactic
jokes.explanation: The genre beat (dramatic pause before the reveal) is well-executed, and the reveal being 'Magnitude' is a perfect Community joke — it rewards long-time viewers and uses the show's own mythology as punchline. The gap between buildup and payoff is beautifully calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Listen, in this town, trust is like a house of cards built on a foundation of sand during an earthquake.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And I'm the only one who can read the map that doesn't exist.

jokes.text: Magnitude's alibi explanation followed by: 'Pop pop!'
jokes.setup: Magnitude delivers a convoluted alibi about a stolen backpack — complex, slightly suspicious.
jokes.punchline: 'Pop pop!' — Magnitude's catchphrase, deployed as the button on his entire statement. His identity is so thoroughly his catchphrase that it ends even serious moments.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character economy — Magnitude's entire comedic existence is compressed into two words. The joke works because the alibi is complicated enough to seem somewhat dramatic, and then 'Pop pop!' resets everything. High character integration (9.0) because this joke literally cannot be told by or about anyone else. The catchphrase as punctuation to serious content is a durable running-gag structure.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'll enhance this photo for the investigation.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: There. I've made it sepia tone.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That should help.

jokes.text: The backpack sting operation — Troy and Abed leave a bag on a table and go to 'the restroom' to wait.
jokes.setup: The group determines whoever stole Magnitude's backpack was a library thief. Troy notes 'only one way to catch a dirtbag like that.'
jokes.punchline: The camera presumably shows them setting the bag trap and surveilling from a distance — a perfectly executed cop-show beat applied to community college library theft.
jokes.explanation: Good genre-beat joke — the procedural trappings applied to mundane crime. Loses points because the visual execution isn't described in enough detail to score higher; it functions as connective tissue for the Star-Burns reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What's 2 plus 2?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? I'm great at other things! I'm an excellent dancer and I'm really good at psychology.

jokes.text: Star-Burns reveals himself as the backpack thief and Troy launches into a 'bad cop' routine: 'Dead yam, big deal. Order some ketchup.' / 'That doesn't make sense. You don't order ketchup. It's a condiment!'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed have set up a good cop/bad cop routine. Troy is bad cop.
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'bad cop' taunting is completely incoherent ('Order some ketchup' has zero menace or logic) and Star-Burns correctly calls it out: 'That doesn't make sense. You don't order ketchup. It's a condiment!'
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke. Troy's bad cop routine failing because his threats are logistically incoherent ('order some ketchup' as a threat) is a great character moment — Troy is so earnest in the genre that he doesn't notice his taunts make no sense. Star-Burns fact-checking 'you don't order ketchup, it's a condiment' is the perfect response: treating Troy's bad cop line not as threatening but as categorically wrong. The condiment lecture is a wonderful escalation. High quotability because 'it's a condiment!' is a genuinely memorable line.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: So who checked out the key?

dialogue.speaker: Magnitude
dialogue.line: Pop pop!

jokes.text: Good cop/bad cop reversal: 'I'm a good cop.' / 'Oh, good.' / 'You can trust me.' — then the suspect immediately sees through it.
jokes.setup: After Troy is walked off, Abed steps in as 'good cop.'
jokes.punchline: Star-Burns is completely undeceived: 'I'm not falling for that. And you got nothing on me. And I don't have to stay here, 'cause you're not cops.' — the genre illusion is punctured by the most obvious possible critique.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in how quickly the genre fantasy collapses — Abed's 'you can trust me' barely has time to land before Star-Burns dismantles it with reality. The 'you're not cops' line is a great meta-deflation of the entire episode's premise. Well-structured, good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Magnitude
dialogue.line: Pop pop!

jokes.text: 'He's right. You're not cops. I'd say our hands are tied, but we basically have no hands.'
jokes.setup: Star-Burns correctly identifies that Troy and Abed have no authority.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response acknowledges the powerlessness with a self-aware metaphor: 'we basically have no hands' — which is both literally true (no legal authority) and a kind of meta-comment on the genre fantasy the episode has been running.
jokes.explanation: The line 'we basically have no hands' is a good Jeff riff — slightly poetic, self-aware, delivered with the casual eloquence that is his brand. The 'tied hands' idiom subverted into 'no hands at all' is a compact structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Order some ketchup.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait — we're at a crime scene. Why would we order ketchup?

jokes.text: The yam forensics report: 'This level of smushing is consistent with someone stepping on the yam after it was dropped.' / 'So whoever did this was angry.' / 'Hey, I just cut 'em open. You want motive, talk to a shrink.'
jokes.setup: The group visits the biology lab for a forensic analysis of the destroyed yam.
jokes.punchline: The lab tech speaks in full CSI autopsy mode — 'smushing is consistent with,' 'you need a boot' — applied to a vegetable. When Abed suggests 'motive,' the tech deflects: 'Hey, I just cut 'em open.' Perfect procedural role-separation.
jokes.explanation: The forensics scene is a great sustained parody beat. 'This level of smushing' is a wonderful phrase that works because 'smushing' is not a forensic term. The scene earns points for committing to the bit fully — the tech doesn't wink at the camera. 'You need a boot' as the clinical conclusion is funny because it's both technically correct and completely obvious.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, Troy, Troy. You need to take a deep breath. You're a champion. Champions don't get rattled.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not rattled!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're doing that thing where you get all high-pitched. That's what you do when you're scared. Remember when we played Paintball? You were terrified and you sounded like a dolphin.

jokes.text: 'You need more than gravity. You need a boot.'
jokes.setup: The forensic analysis of the yam smashing needs a dramatic conclusion.
jokes.punchline: 'You need a boot' — delivered as if it's the conclusion of a complex forensic calculation, when it's actually the most obvious thing in the world.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words, delivered with gravitas. The humor is entirely in the register gap: a full forensic procedure concluded with 'you need a boot,' which everyone already knew. It parodies how procedurals over-elaborate to arrive at obvious conclusions.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Good cop, bad cop. Classic interrogation technique. I'll be the good cop.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, my friend here is going to be very hard on you, but I'm going to be nice. We're on the same team.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. Thanks, Abed. I appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So, you want to tell me what really happened?

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure. Whatever you need to know.

jokes.text: 'Well, whoever did do this does owe you guys a letter.' / 'An "A."' — pause for the pun to land.
jokes.setup: Jeff says the guilty party owes the group a letter — clearly setting up something.
jokes.punchline: Annie: 'An "A"' — both a letter of the alphabet (fulfilling Jeff's setup) and the grade they want. Double meaning, cleanly executed.
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical wordplay. The setup is slightly telegraphed ('a letter' is a known setup for this exact punchline) which prevents it from scoring higher, but it's well-executed and the pause before 'An A' gives it the right beat.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Wait a second... you guys aren't real cops.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Real cops don't wear matching outfits from the Gap.

jokes.text: 'We named the yam "Pam."' / 'It rhymed.'
jokes.setup: The group reflects on the seriousness of the crime in the lab.
jokes.punchline: Troy reveals they named the yam 'Pam,' followed by the most basic possible justification: 'It rhymed.' The name and reasoning are both touchingly, hilariously mundane.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most purely delightful jokes. 'Pam' is funny. 'It rhymed' as the total justification — delivered completely straight — is funnier. The structure is perfect: name reveal (beat), explanation (beat), nothing more needed. It humanizes the yam, retroactively raises the stakes of the investigation, and captures Troy and Abed's particular brand of earnest weirdness. High quotability because it's a complete, freestanding joke anyone can reference.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We have no authority here. We're like a government that can't pass legislation, a tree that can't photosynthesize, a Coldplay album that nobody wants to listen to.

dialogue.speaker: Other
dialogue.line: Did you just compare us to Coldplay?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm trying to make a point about powerlessness. Work with me.

jokes.text: 'Oh, so now you're finding your softness? I say do what you have to do. It's too late to get compassionate. We only have time to get justice.'
jokes.setup: Annie expresses ethical reservations about breaking into a locker.
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a cop-show speech about justice vs. compassion — with complete sincerity — in service of breaking into a school locker over a yam. The genre rhetoric is applied to the most trivial possible stakes.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'justice' speech is a good genre-parody beat — the rhetoric of a climactic cop-show confrontation applied to academic dishonesty and a vegetable. Rewatch bonus because the same speech structure is later echoed by Annie in the trial scene (a callback that makes the moment retroactively funnier).

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Hey, uh, guys? I'm right here. You know that, right?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? Oh, Star-Burns, we weren't—

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: No, no, I get it. You're having a secret conversation. In front of me. The guy with the star-shaped burns on his face. Subtle.

jokes.text: Annie breaking into Star-Burns's locker using the pretext of 'hearing a kitten meowing': 'I really shouldn't be doing this.' / 'And you're sure you heard a kitten meowing in here?' / 'Not anymore, so hurry up.'
jokes.setup: Annie said breaking into a locker isn't ethical, but is now breaking into it.
jokes.punchline: The kitten pretext is both implausible and barely constructed — 'Not anymore, so hurry up' abandons the fiction entirely.
jokes.explanation: Annie's hypocrisy is played perfectly — she protests ethics, then immediately constructs the most tissue-thin possible excuse. 'Not anymore, so hurry up' is especially good because it shows the fiction was always just pro forma. Character-consistent: Annie will do anything for an A.

dialogue.speaker: Lab Technician
dialogue.line: No, this kind of damage could only come from repeated, deliberate trauma. It's like... it's like Josef Mengele, but for yams.

jokes.text: Star-Burns's locker contents: 'Whoa, Nelly!' — the implied visual of whatever is in that locker.
jokes.setup: Jeff suggested breaking into Star-Burns's locker because 'you'll find enough dirt to bury him.'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's reaction ('Whoa, Nelly!') implies the locker contains something spectacularly damning. The specific contents are not revealed here — the joke is the reaction and the audience's imagination.
jokes.explanation: Decent visual-gag setup — the unexplained reaction is a classic comedy technique. The payoff will come later (the meth lab revelation). 'Whoa, Nelly' is a dated exclamation that works for Jeff because it's the kind of archaic expression he'd use for comic effect. Rewatch bonus because the later meth lab reveal recontextualizes this.

dialogue.speaker: Lab Technician
dialogue.line: It takes a very specific amount of force to damage a yam that badly. I'd estimate approximately 300 pounds of pressure concentrated on a single point.

dialogue.speaker: Lab Technician
dialogue.line: Based on the depth and pattern of the bruising, I can only conclude one thing: somebody wore a really heavy shoe.

jokes.text: 'Clean up on aisle "busted."'
jokes.setup: Star-Burns's locker contains incriminating material and he's about to be caught.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'clean up on aisle busted' — a supermarket announcement pun applied to law enforcement, delivered as a one-liner zinger.
jokes.explanation: Decent one-liner — the 'aisle' pun with 'busted' is a clean construction. Loses points because it's a relatively generic pun without much character specificity; Jeff could get sharper than this.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: A love letter? That's so romantic! I'd give that an A!

jokes.text: Two characters both try to say 'Why do they always run?' simultaneously: 'Why do they always r...' / 'Why do they always...' / 'You go ahead.' / 'Why do they always run?' / 'There you go.'
jokes.setup: Star-Burns runs from them — the classic TV-cop scenario where the suspect flees.
jokes.punchline: Both Jeff and Abed reach for the same clichéd cop-show line simultaneously, have to negotiate who delivers it, then one finally says it. A callback to the earlier 'we can't both do the zinger' moment.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. The first time (Troy/Abed, 'Survey says' / 'we can't both do the zinger') established the pattern; this iteration escalates it because (1) now it's Jeff and Abed — different pairing, (2) they've apparently both absorbed so much procedural TV that they reach for the same stock line, and (3) the negotiation ('you go ahead') and delivery ('there you go') adds a layer of mundane courtesy to the meta-joke. Rewatch bonus because the pattern is funnier on second viewing.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We named our yam Yamanda.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You see, it's a yam... and Amanda... they rhyme.

jokes.text: Annie asking Jeff to kiss her as a cover: 'Kiss me!' / 'What?' / 'I'll explain later.' / 'The explanation isn't the issue.'
jokes.setup: Annie needs to create a distraction in a classic genre-spy/cop scenario and asks Jeff to kiss her.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response — 'The explanation isn't the issue' — brilliantly reveals that Jeff's issue isn't confusion but something else entirely (presumably complicated feelings about Annie), delivered as flustered understatement.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest character-comedy moments. 'The explanation isn't the issue' is a perfect Jeff line — it's evasive, it's eloquent, and it reveals more than he intends. The structure is excellent: Annie's pulpy spy-scenario demand → Jeff's reflexive 'What?' (expected beat) → Annie's 'I'll explain later' (expected beat) → then Jeff's response which completely reframes the exchange. The comedic surprise is that his issue isn't with the cover story, it's with the act itself. Rewatch bonus because the Jeff/Annie relationship arc makes this funnier retroactively.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Hey Garrett, you look hungry. You want half my sandwich?

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Really? That's so nice of you!

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Yeah man, here take the whole thing. And my chips too.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Wow, thank you!

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: And my drink. And my dessert. Actually, you know what? Take my whole lunch. I'm not even hungry anymore.

jokes.text: Star-Burns's confession: 'I swiped some beakers for the meth lab that I'm building in the trunk of my car. But that's it. I didn't kill any yam.'
jokes.setup: Star-Burns is caught and pressured into confessing what he was doing in the biology room.
jokes.punchline: He casually reveals he's building a meth lab in his trunk — a Walter White reference — presented as if it's significantly less serious than yam murder.
jokes.explanation: Great escalation joke — the reveal of actual criminal activity (meth lab) as lesser than the alleged crime (yam murder) perfectly inverts the episode's stakes. 'But that's it, I didn't kill any yam' as a moral defense ('I only run a meth lab') is excellent. Character integration is high because Star-Burns's entire characterization is 'clearly shady person in the background.' This also sets up the episode's final beat (the meth lab explosion). Rewatch bonus for that payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me you broke into someone's house because of a kitten?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Had to. It was stuck in the walls.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: For how long?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Three weeks?! Abed, that kitten is definitely dead.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Pinky swear: 'Will you tell our teacher who it was? If you promise I won't get in trouble for stealing that meth lab stuff.' / 'Sure, whatever.' / 'Fine.' / 'Pinky swear?'
jokes.setup: Star-Burns will give up the real culprit if he gets immunity for his meth lab theft.
jokes.punchline: He wants a 'pinky swear' — the most childish possible form of agreement — to seal a deal protecting a drug criminal. Applied to community college procedural, it's perfect.
jokes.explanation: The 'pinky swear' as legally binding immunity agreement is funny and also sets up Professor Kane's later defense of the pinky swear's moral authority — which is the episode's best thematic joke. Rewatch bonus because the pinky swear becomes central to the trial scene.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Eureka!

jokes.text: Pinky swear as legal instrument: Star-Burns demands a 'pinky swear' that he won't get in trouble — and Jeff agrees
jokes.setup: Star-Burns will give up the real culprit if he gets immunity
jokes.punchline: He demands a pinky swear — a kindergarten gesture — as the binding legal guarantee, and Jeff actually does it
jokes.explanation: The pinky swear becomes a plot-critical comedic device — it matters later when Kane defends its honor. The setup here is funny on its own (Jeff, a lawyer, pinky swearing with Star-Burns) but gains more value retroactively.

dialogue.speaker: Store Announcer
dialogue.line: Attention shoppers, we have a blue light special on aisle seven.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You have the right to remain in the store. Anything you shoplift can and will be used against you in a court of law.

jokes.text: Todd Miranda rights parody: 'Todd Jacobson, you have the right to do whatever you want. Nothing you say or do can be used against you by anyone, but we'd really like it if you came with us. Please and thank you.'
jokes.setup: Troy is asked to deliver Miranda rights to Todd — but they have no actual authority
jokes.punchline: The 'rights' are entirely inverted — maximum freedom, polite requests instead of legal compulsion — while maintaining the grave procedural cadence
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The inverted Miranda rights is a brilliantly constructed bit: it maintains the FORM of Miranda (solemn delivery, legal cadence, formal address) while inverting every CONTENT element to reflect their actual powerlessness. 'Please and thank you' as the finale is perfect. The joke has excellent structure, originality, and character integration — only Troy, the enthusiastic genre-performer without real understanding, would deliver this with such sincere authority. Strongly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We've got a 10-31 in progress! We need to set up a perimeter, call for backup, get the—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're gonna need to create a net, a—a dragnet, a—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Perimeter.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're gonna need to set up a perimeter!

jokes.text: Professor Kane's 'hearing' — both sides present to the biology class as judge.
jokes.setup: Jeff brings the yam case to Professor Kane, who decides the class will serve as jury.
jokes.punchline: Kane convening a quasi-trial in a biology class over a broken yam — with an actual Army colonel showing up as defense counsel — is an absurdist escalation that the episode commits to fully.
jokes.explanation: The structural joke of the whole middle section — a biology class becoming a courtroom with an Army colonel defending a veteran against yam charges — is well-executed. The commitment to the bit is admirable, even if individual lines here score lower than the cumulative effect.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Don't call the cops!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Look, I'm sorry, I'm sorry!

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Just... just don't tell anyone!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, are you trying to kiss me right now?

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: It's a distraction technique!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, first of all, your breath smells like a bong made of pepperoni.

jokes.text: Colonel Archwood's introduction: 'I'm Lieutenant Colonel Archwood, United States Army. I had the pleasure of commanding this young man in Iraq. I'm staying on his couch this weekend while I'm in town for a wedding.'
jokes.setup: Colonel Archwood steps in to defend Todd with full military gravitas.
jokes.punchline: His imposing credentials are undercut by his weekend plans: 'I'm staying on his couch while I'm in town for a wedding.' The gap between Lieutenant Colonel authority and couch-surfing is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good bathos joke — the buildup of credentials ('Lieutenant Colonel,' 'commanded in Iraq,' 'licensed attorney,' 'veteran of two wars') followed by 'I'm staying on his couch' deflates the pomposity. The couch detail is specific enough to be genuinely funny, not just a generic undercut.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Yeah, so I've been cooking meth in my car. It's just a hobby, you know? Like some people build model airplanes.

jokes.text: Professor Kane defends the pinky swear: 'Yo, man, you spent your life in the army. I spent mine in prison. Two places where a man's word is only as good as his uniform. Now out here, it's supposed to be different. And in my class, it will be.'
jokes.setup: Colonel Archwood dismisses the pinky swear agreement as beneath consideration.
jokes.punchline: Kane defends the pinky swear by invoking his prison time — an unexpected credential that both punctures Archwood's military authority AND reveals Kane's backstory. The punchline is 'in my class, it will be' — turning a legally absurd position into a principled moral stance.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and its most surprising character moment. The structure is perfect: Archwood's military credentials are met with prison credentials — equal weight, different context. The line 'Two places where a man's word is only as good as his uniform' is a genuinely sharp observation that earns its comedy through truth rather than absurdity. The payoff ('in my class, it will be') reframes the pinky swear as a civilizing principle rather than a childish gesture. This is the kind of joke that works as both comedy and character development simultaneously. Kane's prison backstory makes him more compelling while making the defense of a pinky swear hilarious.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: I'll only accept immunity if you swear on a stack of comic books and pinky swear.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, you're facing felony charges. We need to be serious about this.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: Serious? Fine. Cross your heart AND hope to die, stick a needle in your eye.

jokes.text: 'A man's gotta have a code.'
jokes.setup: Kane has just delivered his principled defense of the pinky swear.
jokes.punchline: He punctuates it with 'A man's gotta have a code' — a line so stock it would be a cliché if not perfectly deployed as the button on a genuinely surprising speech.
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly placed. The line is a cliché, but Kane earns it by having actually demonstrated a code — the words land as genuine character statement rather than empty genre rhetoric. Gets rewatch bonus because Jeff uses the same phrase later when reversing course, making it a thematic throughline.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Todd, we need to talk about your basket weaving.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: What about it?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's a lie. You don't actually weave baskets. You just tell people you do while you sit in the corner and practice your lying.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: That's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're right. I apologize. Basket weaving and lying are two separate hobbies, and you're equally terrible at both.

jokes.text: Abed's 'bad cop' breakdown: 'That what you guys do in here? You push your little papers and you make your little speeches, and in the end another dirtbag walks? Huh? Huh?!' / 'Abed! Abed! Walk it off!'
jokes.setup: Star-Burns has fled, their witness is gone, and the case seems lost.
jokes.punchline: Abed completely breaks character and delivers a full 'frustrated detective' meltdown — 'push your little papers' — requiring Troy to repeat the earlier 'walk it off' routine. The parody is now so complete that Abed has absorbed the breakdown trope.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and escalation. The 'walk it off' bit was established with Troy as the hot cop needing cooling down; now Abed — typically the calm analytical one — has completely lost it, requiring Troy to manage him. The role reversal is funny, the speech ('push your little papers') is a perfect hard-boiled cliché in the mouth of a media-obsessed film student, and 'I'm sorry about my partner. He's been on edge ever since we switched' as the button is a great punch. Rewatch bonus because the 'switched' line is a callback to their earlier cop-role discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You have the right to remain silent. Oh wait, no, that's not right. Um, you have the right to talk a lot. And everything you say will be used to help you in court.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And you have the right to a lawyer, but if you can't afford one, that's cool, we'll just figure something out.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Also, would you mind coming down to the station? Only if you want to, though. No pressure.

jokes.text: Troy's explanation: 'I'm sorry about my partner. He's been on edge ever since we switched.'
jokes.setup: Abed has just had a full bad-cop meltdown, and Troy is apologizing for him.
jokes.punchline: 'Ever since we switched' — implying they recently traded cop roles, which both explains Abed's behavior within the genre and is a funny real-world observation about their friendship dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Abed meltdown scene. 'Ever since we switched' works as both procedural excuse and genuine insight — Troy switched from bad cop to good cop, Abed from good to bad, and the transition destabilized Abed. The earnestness with which Troy delivers cop-show logic as real explanation is very Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: A pinky swear is a legally binding contract.

dialogue.speaker: Colonel Archwood
dialogue.line: This is why I have no respect for the civilian legal system.

jokes.text: Annie mirrors Jeff's earlier speech back at him: 'Now you find your softness? It's eat or be eaten when that's convenient, but when the going gets tough, Winger gets nervous, huh? We only have time to get justice.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is now reluctant to present their case. Earlier, he used the 'justice vs. softness' rhetoric to push Annie.
jokes.punchline: Annie throws his exact words back at him — 'now you find your softness,' 'we only have time to get justice' — verbatim, exposing the hollowness of Jeff's earlier moral posturing.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's structurally finest jokes. The callback works because Annie has heard Jeff use rhetorical speeches to get what he wants enough times that she's learned to do it back to him. The humor is in the perfect parroting ('Winger gets nervous, huh?' as the specific twist on his syntax) and the exposure that Jeff's moral speeches are performance, not conviction. High structure score because the callback is set up and paid off across a significant portion of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: You know, I spent time in both the military and prison. And I'll tell you, they're not that different.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: In both places, how you look is everything. It's all about appearance and credibility.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: In the military, you've got your uniform, your medals, your bearing. In prison, you've got your tattoos, your scars, your reputation.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: Either way, nobody cares what you actually know. They just care what you look like you know.

jokes.text: Todd's heroic backstory: 'I disarmed the I.E.D. and returned the child to his mother. She offered to give me her only possession... a wooden chair... but I refused. I was only doing my duty and we had plenty of chairs at the base.'
jokes.setup: Colonel Archwood is painting Todd as a war hero with a moving story of valor.
jokes.punchline: The story of heroism deflates at the end: Todd refused a war widow's chair because 'we had plenty of chairs at the base' — the most practical and un-heroic possible reason to refuse a gift.
jokes.explanation: Classic bathos structure — genuinely moving setup (child returned to mother, woman gives only possession) punctured by Todd's completely practical logistics. 'We had plenty of chairs at the base' is the perfect anti-heroic reason: not modesty, not principle, just supply adequacy. The specificity of 'wooden chair' as the heroic gift makes the deflation even better.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: I've spent my entire career fighting against the corruption of educational institutions by outside forces. When the yam case came to my desk, I had a choice: compromise my principles for personal gain, or stand firm for what's right.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: I chose integrity. I rejected the yam case entirely.

jokes.text: Archwood's witness attack: 'A man who for all we know is a holocaust-denying, 9/11 pedophile.' / 'Objection.' / 'Withdrawn.'
jokes.setup: Archwood is discrediting Star-Burns's character as a witness.
jokes.punchline: He invents a string of the worst possible character defamations — 'holocaust-denying, 9/11 pedophile' — and immediately withdraws them, perfectly mimicking the courtroom tactic of planting ideas that can't be unplanted.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest legal-parody jokes. The list of accusations — 'holocaust-denying, 9/11 pedophile' — is carefully constructed to combine the two most toxic political crimes with a completely different category of crime, making the combo maximally outrageous while still following the rhythm of legal character assassination. The 'Objection' / 'Withdrawn' exchange is perfect genre parody. High originality because the specific word combo is unexpected and carefully chosen.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: You see, I have principles. I don't compromise them for anyone or anything.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: As Omar Little once said, 'You come at the king, you best not miss.' And I live by that philosophy.

jokes.text: Rapid fire objections parody: 'Objection, she's clearly ramping up to something.' / 'Objection, that's not a real objection.' / 'Objection, I hate the both of you.'
jokes.setup: Classic courtroom objection battle
jokes.punchline: The objections escalate from procedural to meta ('not a real objection') to purely personal ('I hate the both of you') — Kane's final objection is completely outside courtroom procedure
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalating three-beat structure. Each objection degrades one step further from legal form: Archwood's is strategic, Annie's is procedurally correct, Kane's is purely emotional. 'Objection, I hate the both of you' is an excellent line — Kane breaking from his judge role to express sheer exasperation is unexpected and very funny. The structure alone earns it; the economy (three lines, three escalating beats) is tight. Earns the 8.4.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey. It's okay. Just breathe. In through your nose, out through your mouth.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I can't! Everything is terrible!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, Troy, Troy. Look at me. You're going to be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: How do you know that?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because I'm going to help you through this. Just like you helped me.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay. Okay. Thank you, Abed.

jokes.text: Annie's cross-examination setup: 'Tell me, Todd, do you consider yourself a hero?' — long pause — 'Oh. Of course not. A hero doesn't call himself a hero...'
jokes.setup: Annie begins her cross-examination with an apparently softening question.
jokes.punchline: Todd falls into the trap of giving a humble, self-aware answer that Annie will use against him — but the immediate comedy is Todd's earnest 'Oh. Of course not. A hero gets called a hero because of what he does.' The pause before his answer implies he almost said yes.
jokes.explanation: Good courtroom drama parody — the 'do you consider yourself a hero?' question is a classic TV attorney's trap. Todd's answer is both straight-man funny (he takes the question very seriously) and sets up Annie's subsequent demolition. Rewatch bonus because knowing where this leads makes Todd's earnest hero-definition more poignant.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm sorry about Abed. He gets a little intense sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not apologizing. And Troy, you're doing that thing where you apologize for me like I'm your emotional support animal.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: See, this is what I'm talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, Troy. I'M your emotional support animal. Remember? We switched.

jokes.text: Annie's courtroom triple-objection exchange: 'Objection, she's clearly ramping up to something.' / 'Objection, that's not a real objection.' / 'Objection, I hate the both of you.'
jokes.setup: Annie is in the middle of her cross-examination and Archwood objects.
jokes.punchline: The objections escalate from legal to meta ('not a real objection') to personal ('I hate the both of you') — Kane's final objection is completely outside any procedural framework and reveals his exasperation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments and a structurally perfect escalating joke. Three objections, three different categories: (1) legitimate-ish, (2) meta-commentary on the first, (3) pure emotion. The escalation is perfectly calibrated — each step is unexpected and funnier than the last. 'Objection, I hate the both of you' is an instant quotable because it perfectly expresses everyone's feeling about over-lawyered situations. Kane sustaining his own objection is a perfect button. This approaches the 8.0 anchor bar on craft and exceeds it.

dialogue.speaker: Colonel Archwood
dialogue.line: Star-Burns, you're a menace! You're probably involved in identity theft, counterfeiting, and... competitive tickling!

jokes.text: Annie's sustained cross-examination of Todd — the rapid-fire withdrawn questions: 'Is that why you hit your wife? Withdrawn. Is that why you drink and pop pills? Withdrawn. Are you a virgin? Withdrawn.'
jokes.setup: Annie is cross-examining Todd about whether his frustration with the yam made him violent.
jokes.punchline: She fires a series of inflammatory, unrelated, increasingly personal accusations — each immediately withdrawn — planting them anyway. The sequence escalates to 'Are you a virgin?' as a completely non-sequitur accusation, breaking the pattern.
jokes.explanation: Annie mirrors and escalates Archwood's earlier 'withdrawn' tactic but takes it somewhere completely unexpected. 'Is that why you hit your wife? Withdrawn' and 'Is that why you drink and pop pills? Withdrawn' escalate the TV courtroom manipulation effectively, then 'Are you a virgin? Withdrawn' is a perfect genre-breaking non sequitur — it has no logical connection to yam murder and is completely inappropriate even by the standards Annie has established. The character integration is excellent: Annie, normally the ethical one, has fully embraced Jeff's 'get justice' amoral pragmatism. The withdrawn rhythm makes each accusation land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying Todd is a hero? That's amazing! I mean, wow, a real hero in our midst.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Although, now that I think about it, didn't he also steal from the student activities fund? And didn't he start that rumor about Shirley? And isn't he currently failing Spanish?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So I guess what I'm saying is... Todd's not really a hero, is he? He's just a guy who did one good thing surrounded by a mountain of terrible decisions.

jokes.text: Annie's closing appeal: 'Come on, Todd. Stop disappointing me. Defuse the I.E.D. of dishonesty.'
jokes.setup: Annie is appealing to Todd's military sense of duty to get him to confess.
jokes.punchline: 'Defuse the I.E.D. of dishonesty' — mixing military metaphor with abstract virtue in a phrase so strained it becomes accidentally brilliant.
jokes.explanation: Annie fully committing to a strained military metaphor that makes almost no sense but sounds profound is a perfect character moment. The phrase 'I.E.D. of dishonesty' is so earnestly over-constructed that it becomes genuinely funny. It also works because Annie has absorbed enough procedural rhetoric in this episode to generate her own clichés. High quotability because the phrase is memorable precisely for being so weird.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Todd has a perfect record. Not a single blemish.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, except for one thing that completely ruins everything.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: He's terrible at saying goodbye.

jokes.text: Todd's confession triggers Troy's celebration: 'Booyah! That's how it's done!' — immediately followed by dancing/singing.
jokes.setup: Todd confesses to dropping the yam.
jokes.punchline: Troy's disproportionate victory celebration — 'Booyah!' + a song + presumably dancing — in a classroom biology trial context.
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat — Troy's enthusiasm is always reliable comedy and 'Booyah!' fits his character well. Loses points because it doesn't add much beyond the expected victory-celebration response.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. I object to your tone. And your shoes. And the way you're breathing. Also, you're a bad person. Actually, no, I take that back. And the shoes thing. And the breathing. I withdraw all of it.

jokes.text: 'Always have an exit strategy.'
jokes.setup: Following the celebration, Annie drops a cool one-liner.
jokes.punchline: 'Always have an exit strategy' — a military/tactical maxim delivered by Annie in full self-satisfied attorney mode, applied to a yam confession in a biology class.
jokes.explanation: Annie's post-victory cool-girl one-liner — she's been fully transformed by the procedural genre. The military phrase applied to community college trial work is consistent with the episode's theme. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Colonel
dialogue.line: Be quiet, Todd.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well you're a... a... SANDWICH PANTS!

jokes.text: Jeff's sidebar reversal: 'Todd didn't do it.' / 'Um, he just confessed, dummy.' / 'He said the jar burned him? It doesn't make any sense. People don't half-confess to crimes.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is celebrating Todd's confession. Jeff pumps the brakes.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's argument against accepting the confession ('people don't half-confess to crimes') is delivered just after they've spent the entire episode using TV-procedural logic, making his sudden evidentiary standard both more principled and more absurd.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's character arc in this episode is well-served here — his reversal is played as genuine moral growth (the episode's only sincere character moment) but framed as professional reasoning. The humor comes from the fact that after all the procedural genre play, Jeff's genuinely good argument is treated as unreasonable by everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: Sir, I'm launching a full-scale investigation into the yam situation. I've got reconnaissance teams sweeping the perimeter, supply lines being audited, and I'm treating this like we're storming the beaches of Normandy.

dialogue.speaker: Colonel
dialogue.line: Todd, it's a yam. In the cafeteria.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: With all due respect, sir, there are no small yams in the battle for truth!

jokes.text: Jeff's character-break speech: 'Don't be like me. A man's got to have a code. I can only assume there is a female equivalent to that. A "codette" or something.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is making a sincere moral argument to Annie about not accepting a false win.
jokes.punchline: He invokes Kane's 'a man's gotta have a code,' then immediately undermines his own sincerity by tacking on 'I can only assume there is a female equivalent to that. A "codette" or something' — the trivializing afterthought deflates his moment of genuine growth.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and Jeff's funniest line. The structure is perfect: Jeff has a genuine character moment, quotes Kane with sincerity, then immediately hedges his own masculine framing with an uncomfortable awareness of its limitations — but the hedge ('a codette or something') is so clumsy and self-undermining that it becomes funnier than if he'd stayed sincere OR been fully self-aware. 'Codette' is a genuinely funny word construction. This is Jeff Winger in one joke: wanting to be sincere, being eloquent, then revealing his feet of clay in a single throwaway word. High character integration: only Jeff would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You need to tell the truth, Todd. Just rip the band-aid off.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: It's not that simple, Annie. This is like a military operation. I need to plan my approach, scout the terrain, establish supply lines...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Todd, that's not a metaphor for confession, that's just you avoiding it.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: I'm going in at dawn.

jokes.text: 'Why was it so hard for all of us to grow a yam? It's just a stupid yam in a stupid jar. We're all fully-grown adults failing a kindergarten project.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is making closing arguments and the episode needs to arrive at its real truth.
jokes.punchline: 'We're all fully-grown adults failing a kindergarten project' — the meta-commentary on the episode's stakes, delivered as if it's a profound observation, is both accurate and deflating.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's closer is characteristically self-aware and deflating — it acknowledges the absurdity of the entire episode's premise in a line that is both a good joke and genuine truth. 'Stupid yam in a stupid jar' is an elegantly repetitive phrasing. The observation is Greendale-specific in the best way.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I won! I won! I won!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Whoo! Yeah! Uh-huh! That's right!

jokes.text: Kane's objection to Jeff's speech: 'Can I object?' / 'I'll allow it.' / 'Sustained.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is making a closing argument and Kane interjects.
jokes.punchline: Kane does his 'I'll allow it / Sustained' bit again — his own self-contradictory ruling has become a running gag.
jokes.explanation: Second use of Kane's self-contradictory ruling. Loses some freshness from the first use but still works as an established running gag. The smile of recognition from the audience carries the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Colonel Archwood
dialogue.line: You better confess, Todd, or I'm calling your mother.

jokes.text: Annie produces her own yam: 'Hey, that's mine! Look at it. Everyone look. Smushed without being stepped on.'
jokes.setup: Jeff's closing argument suggests the yam's roots were dead before hitting the ground — a new theory
jokes.punchline: Annie produces her own yam as physical evidence in the middle of class — 'everyone look' — to demonstrate the boiling theory
jokes.explanation: Annie whipping out a yam in the middle of a mock trial as courtroom evidence is an absurd visual moment. The escalation from 'argument' to 'physical yam demonstration' is funny and characteristically Annie.

dialogue.speaker: Colonel Archwood
dialogue.line: Remember, son, the key to any successful operation is proper reconnaissance and tactical positioning. You need to establish dominance in the social hierarchy before engaging the target.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: Um, I was just trying to ask her out.

dialogue.speaker: Colonel Archwood
dialogue.line: Exactly. First, you survey the perimeter, identify potential obstacles, and execute a coordinated strike. It's basic military strategy.

jokes.text: 'Boiling water is the icicle stabbing of yam killing.'
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals that boiling water killed the yam, undetectable because it cools overnight.
jokes.punchline: The icicle-stabbing metaphor — delivered as if it's a known category of crime that everyone should recognize.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best individual line. 'Boiling water is the icicle stabbing of yam killing' scores this high because it's genuinely original, it has a beautiful internal logic (icicle stabbing = untraceable weapon because evidence disappears, boiling water = untraceable because it cools), it's perfectly economical (11 words, complete thought), and it's delivered as dry forensic wisdom. The phrase 'yam killing' as a category of crime is also very funny. This is a quotable line that could become a cultural reference in the right context. It earns its proximity to the 9+ anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to create my own code. It's called the 'Code of Chivalry,' and rule number one is that I get to make up all the rules as I go along.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Rule two: all women must wear tiaras at all times. Rule three: every Friday is 'Compliment Jeff' day.

jokes.text: Jeff's moment of doubt: 'Ooh, but that didn't... Hmm. This yam isn't boiled.' — examining a yam that contradicts his theory.
jokes.setup: Jeff has just confidently revealed his boiling-water theory.
jokes.punchline: He immediately finds a counterexample — an unboiled yam — which makes his dramatic reveal look premature. 'Ooh, but that didn't... Hmm' is perfect deflation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deflation of Jeff's confident revelation — he barely has time to enjoy his Sherlock moment before his own theory is undermined. 'Ooh, but that didn't...' is a great sound of an eloquent man running out of words. This sets up the actual reveal (Vicki's yam untouched because Neil loved her) which is the episode's funniest final twist.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, so we've been investigating this for three weeks because someone ate a yogurt from the break room fridge?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: A yogurt that was already expired.

jokes.text: Neil's confession: 'I boiled the yams. Vicki's yam never sprouted and I didn't want her to fail, so I threw off the grading curve so she wouldn't have to go to summer school and we can finally have sex in my parents' cabin. God forgive me, I did it for love!'
jokes.setup: Neil is revealed as the actual yam boiler.
jokes.punchline: His motive escalates from sweet (didn't want her to fail) to practical (summer school) to frankly carnal (sex in his parents' cabin) to melodramatic ('God forgive me, I did it for love!') — the trajectory from romantic to base to operatic is perfectly calibrated.
jokes.explanation: The episode's big comedic payoff and one of its finest jokes. The escalation from love → summer school → parents' cabin sex → 'God forgive me' is perfectly structured. Each beat is funnier than the last, with 'we can finally have sex in my parents' cabin' being the moment the room erupts (the mundane logistics of a planned sexual encounter as the actual motivation for yam murder). 'God forgive me, I did it for love!' as the operatic button on a confession about boiling vegetable matter is pitch-perfect melodrama. This is a 9.0 on structure — the escalation is exactly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We're not very smart, are we?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No. No, we're not.

jokes.text: 'Holy crap. We are definitely dissecting pine cones next year.'
jokes.setup: Neil has just confessed to boiling everyone's yams for love and sex logistics.
jokes.punchline: Kane's response — the most practical possible reaction — immediately moves past the drama to curriculum reform: pine cones next year, because yams generate too much crime.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and Kane's finest moment. The humor is in the gap between the emotional chaos just witnessed and Kane's completely practical response — he doesn't address the relationship drama, the boiling, the honor of Todd, or any of it. He just concludes: pine cones are safer curriculum. 'We are definitely dissecting pine cones next year' is a perfect teacher line — it implies this happens every year with different vegetables. High character integration: Kane's weary pragmatism is exactly right here.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The murder weapon was so cold, it was like the Arctic and the Sahara had a baby, and that baby was a frozen knife made of liquid nitrogen and regret.

jokes.text: Post-verdict summary: 'After all the politics and procedure, in the end, the case really was about biology. Told you it was an important subject.'
jokes.setup: The yam case is resolved — it was about love, sex, and academic competition.
jokes.punchline: Kane reframes the entire case as vindication of biology as a discipline — 'it really was about biology' (reproduction, desire) — with a smug 'Told you it was an important subject.'
jokes.explanation: Smart thematic callback — the episode's premise (yam project as Law & Order) resolves with the acknowledgment that it really was a biology story all along (sex, reproduction, competition). Kane's dry 'Told you it was an important subject' is a great teacher's smugness. Works both as a joke and as satisfying structural closure.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: See? My theory is working!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The evidence clearly points to...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You! It was you all along!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, that's me. I'm standing right in front of you.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: Star-Burns's death: 'Star-Burns got rear-ended and the meth lab in his trunk exploded. He's dead.' — delivered flat, over a phone call.
jokes.setup: Star-Burns was established as running a meth lab in his car trunk.
jokes.punchline: He's dead. The meth lab exploded when he got rear-ended. The payoff to the earlier Chekhov's gun (meth lab in trunk) is a character death delivered with Shirley's flat matter-of-factness.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most audacious jokes — it kills a recurring character (Star-Burns is a fan-favorite background presence) as a Chekhov's gun payoff. The structure is extraordinary: the meth lab was established as a throwaway detail in a confession scene, and the episode uses it as a final-act gut-punch. The flatness of delivery — Shirley on the phone, matter-of-fact — makes the death funnier and more shocking simultaneously. 'He's dead.' as a two-word button to what should be a dramatic revelation is perfect deadpan. This also sets up a later storyline, but as a standalone joke it's exceptional for its structural boldness.

dialogue.speaker: Neil
dialogue.line: I have something to confess. I murdered those yams.

dialogue.speaker: Neil
dialogue.line: But that's not all. I'm in love with you.

dialogue.speaker: Neil
dialogue.line: My parents have a cabin upstate, and I've been thinking about us there, in the hot tub, and... well, my parents use that hot tub too, and they're very active people.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed's bunk bed conversation: 'Why do you think they call them bunk beds? Where's the word bunk come from?' / 'I think it comes from the word bunker.'
jokes.setup: Troy notes that he and Abed are best friends sharing a bunk bed and should be having bunk bed conversations.
jokes.punchline: The conversation they launch into is about the etymology of 'bunk' — the most Troy-and-Abed-appropriate trivial deep-dive possible, delivered with the seriousness of a philosophy seminar.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Troy-and-Abed character moment. The concept of 'bunk bed conversations' as a genre they're consciously cultivating is delightfully specific. Their first topic being etymological speculation about 'bunk' is so perfectly them — earnest, slightly nerdy, completely disconnected from the previous scene's gravity. The scene functions as a tonal reset after Star-Burns's death and characterizes their friendship beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Neil
dialogue.line: I sabotaged the yams. It was me. I did it because... because I wanted to prove that I could commit the perfect crime. A crime so subtle, so perfectly executed, that no one would ever suspect Neil. And I got away with it. For a while.

jokes.text: Troy's fumigation reveal: 'So when is your apartment done being fumigated?' / 'Oh, it was done about a week ago.' / 'Then why are you still here?'
jokes.setup: Troy has apparently been staying with Abed while his apartment is fumigated.
jokes.punchline: The fumigation has been done for a week — Troy has just been staying anyway. Neither of them acknowledges this as strange.
jokes.explanation: Sweet character reveal — Troy has been making excuses to extend his stay with Abed. The joke is the gap between the transparent pretext and the genuine friendship. Neither character addresses the obvious truth, which makes it funnier and more touching. Rewatch bonus because Troy eventually moves in permanently, making this a retroactive setup.

dialogue.speaker: Neil
dialogue.line: Treats yam murder like crime of passion

jokes.text: Troy and Abed bedtime song: '♪ Troy and Abed, off to Dreamland / catching the train to Sleepytown / and when they wake up / the Dean'll be here / staring at you ♪' / 'Sweet deans.' / 'That's nice... I guess.'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are going to sleep in their bunk bed.
jokes.punchline: They sing an original bedtime song — charming and childlike — which incorporates the Dean inexplicably staring at them. 'Sweet deans' as the sign-off. Troy's reaction: 'That's nice... I guess.'
jokes.explanation: Wonderful episode-closer. The bedtime song is pitch-perfect Troy-and-Abed — it has the structure of a genuine lullaby, it's wordlessly sweet, and then it introduces the Dean staring at them in the middle of the night, which is both hilarious and reveals the Dean's creepiness as simply part of their world. 'Sweet deans' as the equivalent of 'sweet dreams' is an excellent pun. Troy's 'That's nice... I guess' captures his perpetual mixed feelings about Abed's odd behavior. High character integration because this song captures both characters' blend of earnestness and weirdness.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Kane
dialogue.line: After witnessing that elaborate yam murder case, I've decided to switch to a simpler biology project.

tmdb_overview: When the yam the study group was growing for biology class is killed, Troy and Abed are on the case.
insight: CSI parody sustains 75 jokes across 45 minutes with expert escalation.
